aula.objetivo: Form and use the pluscuamperfecto («había hablado», «había hecho») to talk about something that had already happened before another moment in the past, with pronouns, negation, questions and markers like «ya» and «todavía no».

blocos.texto: Welcome to B1. At A2 you told stories in the past with the indefinido and the imperfecto, and you already use «he» + participle. Now you'll learn to place one event BEFORE another past event, which makes your stories much clearer.

blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: good news — this tense is English "had + past participle": "I had left", "she had done". Spanish builds it exactly the same way: «había salido», «había hecho». STEP 2: the catch: English "have" is both possession and the auxiliary; Spanish splits them. Possession is «tener», but the auxiliary is ALWAYS «haber». So "I had a car" is «Tenía un coche», but "I had eaten" is «Había comido» — never «tenía comido». STEP 3: the auxiliary is «haber» in the imperfecto: «había, habías, había, habíamos, habíais, habían». Every form has an accent on the «í». STEP 4: then comes the participle: -ar verbs take «-ado» (hablado), -er and -ir verbs take «-ido» (comido, vivido). When the stem ends in a strong vowel (a, e, o), «-ido» takes an accent: «leído, oído, traído, creído, caído». STEP 5: the irregular participles are the same ones you already use with «he»: hecho, dicho, visto, puesto, escrito, abierto, vuelto, roto, muerto, cubierto, resuelto — and their compounds: «deshecho, descrito, devuelto, descubierto». Watch out: Spanish never adds «-ido» to these («escribido», «hacido» don't exist), just as English doesn't say "writed". STEP 6: with «haber», the participle NEVER agrees: «Ella había salido», «Ellas habían salido». STEP 7: the auxiliary and the participle stay together — nothing goes in between. English says "I had ALREADY left", "I had NEVER seen", "I had seen IT"; Spanish moves those words outside: «Ya había salido», «Nunca había visto», «Lo había visto». STEP 8: careful: «había» is also the past of «hay» («había mucha gente» = there were a lot of people). If a participle follows, it's the auxiliary.
blocos.comparacao: English has the same tense: "had + past participle" = «había + participio». Two differences: the auxiliary is «haber», not «tener» (English "have" covers both), and nothing goes between «había» and the participle — English "had already left" is «ya había salido», "had seen it" is «lo había visto».

erros.motivo: The auxiliary in this tense is «haber», not «tener» — English "had" doesn't become «tenía» here.
Every form of «había» takes an accent on the «í».
With «haber», the participle doesn't change for gender or number.

blocos.enunciado: Imagine 8 a.m. yesterday. Say five sentences about what you had already done by then: «A las ocho ya había desayunado. Todavía no había salido de casa…»
Say out loud what you've already done today, with «he» + participle: «He desayunado… He salido…». Then say the participle of hacer, decir, ver, poner and escribir.
